name: Erik Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and have answered payment and delivery calls at this contact centre for eleven years. I finished secondary school and know the ordinary account trail well enough, though I am not the person who trains the leads or solves every unusual case. My wage is low for the job. I have never used AI tools; I read the account history from the first charge to the last.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Kay works short shifts in a hotel laundry, and our children are grown and live on their own. We have less than a month of expenses saved and only a few other centres nearby. Retirement is something we discuss, but I have no checked income figure that lets me give you a date. I remember the caller who was asked to explain the same payment four times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AI Plateau is no excuse to close a payment case before the receipt has been matched. I would ask our staff group to keep proper correction time in the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my calls continue because the small shortcuts do not settle a wrong account. I still worry about the next bill; Kay’s short laundry shifts and our few weeks saved do not leave much space.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep handling payment calls and bring the case of a misposted rent transfer to the staff meeting. In the first year of this small change, I’d sign a joint request for paid correction minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, steady about the work. A closed call cannot move rent money to the right account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which case would you show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show how the receipt and account number differed by one digit. The second caller should not have had to start that story again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would money feel different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kay (my partner) and I would keep our small cash for bills. We would not pretend that a faster script fills the savings jar.

I’d insist on matching **receipts to accounts** before closing a call.
think: I think **payment calls** continue in a mild change.
I fear **low savings** and Kay’s short shifts still leave us exposed.
do: Keep **handling payment calls** and bring a misposted transfer to staff meeting.
Sign a **joint rota request** for paid correction minutes in the first year.
feel: **Anxious** about bills, steady about call work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will answer simple payment questions and leave us the cases where the money is in the wrong place. I would ask other agents to demand written hours for those corrections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my experience may keep me on the harder calls, but it may not keep a full week on the rota. Less than a month saved means even two lost shifts would be felt at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d join the staff letter asking for paid correction hours and keep checking the account trail on my assigned calls. In the first year simple questions move, I’d compare each new rota with the last one and ask the staff group to challenge any cut that leaves reopened cases without paid agents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing hours. Eleven years of work do not make the electricity company wait for payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the letter count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count the reopened transfers, not only the chats the software says it settled. That gives us a reason to ask for staff time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if two shifts disappear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kay (my partner) would see the changed wage on our weekly list. Cutting one restaurant meal would not replace two missing shifts.

say: I’d demand **written correction hours** with other agents as the simple calls move.
I’d count **reopened transfers** beside automated closures.
think: I think my **eleven years** may keep harder calls.
I fear **two lost shifts** would still hurt our household bills.
do: Join **staff letter** for paid correction hours and keep assigned account checks in 2026.
Compare **new rotas** with old and challenge cuts jointly where reopened cases remain.

fieldNote: His **experience** may preserve tasks but not full hours.

steps.text: Join staff letter requesting written paid correction hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the floor AGI by 2028 could trace the payment and make the correction decision itself. Robots around 2031 are later, and a phone shift will not wait for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the centre could lose most payment calls and my wage with them. With less than one month saved and only Kay’s short shifts alongside mine, we would need a new paid week quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d join colleagues in asking for written cut dates and a paid human appeal route, then check the few posted paid contact jobs nearby. If my hours end in the first year after 2028, I’d apply only where written weekly wages and hours cover our essential bills after travel, keeping my present job until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. The next month of bills is closer than a new occupation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must an appeal worker do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask who can actually correct a wrong AI decision, not just take another complaint. The staff request must include that authority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you compare another centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kay (my partner) and I would compare the bus fare and the full week of pay at any other centre. A higher rate for three shifts would not cover five days of bills.

I’d say **2028 thinking AI** threatens calls before robots.
think: I think **most payment calls** could disappear quickly as cheaper AGI reaches the desk.
I know **under one month saved** leaves little search time.
do: Join colleagues’ **written notice request** and inspect posted local contact work in 2026.
Apply after call loss only for **weekly wages** and hours covering bills after travel; leave when signed.
S2.quote: The next month of bills is closer than a new occupation.
fieldNote: His **thin reserve** makes job loss immediate household trouble.
The **group appeal** asks for correction authority and paid time.
Another centre must provide **whole-week pay after travel**.

steps.text: Join coworkers requesting written cuts and paid appeals with correction authority

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives our centre five years to show which human correction jobs it will pay for. I would keep asking through the staff group for actual hours, not training links.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could stay on payment appeals if the work is real, though full thinking AI could check those accounts too. I do not want a course merely to be told that no post exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d keep my assigned payment calls and join the annual staff request for a paid appeal rota. In the first year after 2031, if call hours fall, I’d apply for a posted paid appeals job at a nearby centre only where written weekly wages and hours cover our bills after bus fare; I would leave only after a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with more time to bargain than in the fast case. A training link has no shift attached to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make appeals real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the appeals desk whether it can reverse the account entry itself. If it cannot, the customer remains in the same loop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you reach another centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kay (my partner) would check the late bus home from another centre. We have no savings for repeated taxi rides.

I’d demand **account reversal authority** at any appeals desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives us time to press for paid human corrections every year. I would not treat ten years as proof that everyone my age can stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think Kay and I might still need both wages at 68, because we have not checked what income would follow work. Full thinking AI could still handle payment calls in 2036; robots around 2039 arrive later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking paid payment calls and join the annual staff request for correction hours. If I still need work after 2036 and my shifts fall, I’d seek posted paid contact work within bus reach and move only on a signed offer with written weekly wages and hours covering bills after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious even with a long warning. Our savings would not carry many missed weeks this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide when to stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would sit with Kay (my partner) and check actual later-life income against bills before naming a stopping date. I would not guess that a pension will arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would adult children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have their own households. I would not put their money in our plan unless they offered it and we knew the amount.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the one that frightens me. It could do the payment trail I have spent years learning, and a few weeks of savings would not carry us through a long search. Written notice, paid hours for human corrections, and a real paid alternative would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The customer can show the receipt and still be sent back to the beginning. Someone needs paid time and permission to move the payment to the right account.

headlineQuote: Someone needs paid time and permission to move the payment to the right account.
portrait: At **58**, Erik is an experienced mid-level agent with average skill and secondary-school education.
He and Kay have **grown children**, a lower wage and less than one month saved.
With **few local jobs**, losing paid calls would quickly threaten household bills.
He **never uses AI** and presses coworkers for paid human correction time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could replace the payment tracing that supports his low wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid correction hours and a real paid alternative would help.
